title: Election Night, Hour by Hour: Polls Close and Counting Begins
summary:
On Tuesday, voters across the United States will finish choosing members of Congress and governors, and then the counting begins.

Polls close at different times in different states, starting at 7 p.m. Eastern Time and ending at 1 a.m. Eastern Time, when Alaska finishes. That is why election night unfolds in waves, like a long scoreboard lighting up state by state.

Early attention will go to Georgia and Florida. Georgia has a Senate race and a closely watched governor's race, and Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger has told local news that new laws require counties to report results within an hour of polls closing. Florida also has a governor's race and a Senate race, and, according to the Cook Political Report, seven competitive House races.

As more polls close, attention spreads. Competitive Senate races in North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Maine could help decide control of the Senate. Later, Senate races in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan and Texas will also be watched closely, along with governor's races in states including Arizona.

Control of the House could become clear sooner because of bigger margins, while control of the Senate could take much longer. The margins there are tighter, seven states are especially competitive, and two states use ranked choice voting, which can prolong counting.

California closes later and is described as a slow-counting state, so some of its races may not be called quickly. Alaska is last, and its results could take weeks to be finalized because it uses ranked choice voting.

Vote counting will start Tuesday night, but it could go on for days or even weeks before every close race is settled.
why_it_matters: These races decide who controls the House and the Senate, which shapes the laws the country makes. Learning why results arrive slowly also helps people stay patient instead of expecting every answer on election night.

background_read: On election day in the United States, voters choose members of Congress and governors, and counting begins once polls close.
Polls close at different times in different states, so results arrive in waves across the night rather than all at once.
Control of the House and the Senate depends on the results of many separate races, and close races can take longer to settle.
Some states are slower to count, and ranked choice voting can prolong counting, so some results may take days or weeks to be finalized.
